mcqs.question: A problem asks you to return every stored word that begins with a given prefix. Why does a hash map struggle here while a trie doesn't?
options: Hashing discards the prefix structure of a key, so answering "starts with" requires scanning every stored key
A hash map can only store 26 keys at a time
A trie is always faster than a hash map for any operation
Hash maps cannot store strings, only fixed-size keys
mcqs.explanation: A hash function maps a key to a bucket with no relationship to that key's prefixes, so a hash map has no way to find "all keys starting with X" except checking every key. A trie keeps every prefix as a real, walkable node, which is exactly what that query needs.

mcqs.question: Autocomplete first walks to the prefix's node, then DFS-collects matching words. What determines the cost of the DFS step?
options: The total number of words stored anywhere in the trie
The number of words matching the prefix and their average length, since only that subtree is explored
The length of the typed prefix alone
The depth of the entire trie regardless of the prefix
mcqs.explanation: Once you've walked to the prefix's node, the DFS only explores the subtree beneath it — words outside that subtree are never touched, so cost scales with matches found, not with the trie's total size. The prefix length only bounds the walk to reach that node, a separate cost.

mcqs.question: Word Search II needs to check 1000 dictionary words against a letter board. What makes the single-shared-trie approach faster than running a separate board search per word?
options: It reduces the board size the search has to explore
It sorts the dictionary words alphabetically before searching
Every word's search shares the same pruning: a board path that can't extend into any dictionary word is cut once, for all words at once
It only works because the board happens to be small
mcqs.explanation: A single DFS walking the shared trie alongside the board prunes a dead-end path for every word simultaneously, since the trie node itself encodes which next letters remain viable across the whole dictionary. Running 1000 separate searches repeats that exploration once per word with no sharing.

mcqs.question: In Replace Words, the trie walk for a given word should stop at the FIRST node marked is_end it encounters, rather than continuing to the end of the word. Why?
options: Continuing further would cause an infinite loop
Stopping early is just a minor optimization with no effect on correctness
It doesn't matter which is_end node you stop at — all matches are the same length
The first is_end reached is necessarily the shortest matching root, since the walk proceeds character by character from the start
mcqs.explanation: Because the walk proceeds one character at a time from the beginning of the word, the first is_end node encountered corresponds to the shortest prefix that's a stored root — exactly the answer the problem wants. Continuing past it could match a longer root instead, which is the wrong answer, not just a slower one.

mcqs.question: When walking a binary trie to find the number that maximizes XOR with a given value, which child should you prefer at each bit level?
options: The child matching the current number's bit, since XOR rewards agreement
The child opposite the current number's bit, since XOR is maximized by mismatched bits
Whichever child was inserted first at that level
The child with more descendants, to maximize the search space explored
mcqs.explanation: XOR produces a 1 bit exactly when two bits differ, so maximizing XOR means greedily preferring the opposite bit at every level, falling back to the same-bit child only when no opposite-bit child exists. Preferring matching bits would minimize, not maximize, the result.
